newsitem.title: UK: Mark on hold as EMU optimism grows ahead of summit.
newsitem.headline: Mark on hold as EMU optimism grows ahead of summit.

text.p: The mark held firm against other European currencies, poised for a two-day European summit starting today which was likely to be dominated by discussions on Europe's economic and monetary union.

The European leaders, who are meeting in Amsterdam, looked set to patch up their differences on an EMU pact on budget stability -- which had been seen as a top issue for the summit -- after they held a special meeting on Sunday for that purpose.
The possibility of an agreement on the pact was increasing the prospects of monetary union going ahead with a large number of members and hence a softer single currency.

"People here believe they will reach some sort of compromise, either today or tomorrow, and that will remove one of the barriers for the single currency," said Rob Hayward, economic advisor at Bank of America. "But at the same time, a compromise would make it (EMU) more unstable."

Such an outlook usually pushes the mark lower on the perception that it will turn into a weaker currency when monetary union takes place. But the mark was unfazed by the weekend's developments since the financial markets had been expecting since late last week that EU nations will manage to strike a deal on the stability pact.
The mark was quoted at 3.3747/52 French francs at 0830 GMT against 3.3738/43 in late European trade on Friday. Against the lira, it was at 981.80/00, almost unchanged from Friday.

A likely reason for the mark not weakening much on expectations for the stability pact was that even if this problem were resolved, the currency market saw further turbulence ahead over the EMU project, analysts said.

"There are so many uncertainties still hanging over EMU, at the present time the markets are still confused and will probably remain so for some time," said Elizabeth Legge, senior economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin in London.
"As far as the Europe issue is concerned, it's still very difficult to discern a trend and put money on it," Legge said.

The latest dispute over the stability pact, meant to enforce budget discipline on EMU members, erupted last week when France's new government insisted that more weight be given to EU co-ordination on policies to promote jobs and growth.
Germany, for its part, has opposed a French proposal for a costly drive to promote employment in Europe.
However, EU leaders who attended Sunday's meeting on the stability pact all chorused that a deal was in sight. EU finance ministers are scheduled to meet at 0900 GMT to discuss the pact.

"There is a belief that there will be some sort of compromise, but this is not so much a certainty as it was six weeks ago, before the French elections and the German gold issue," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Investment Bank.
Despite their differences, European leaders' political desire to make monetary union a success was so great that none wanted to risk seriously undermining EMU, analysts said.

"Germany is so politically committed to EMU that it will agree to almost anything, and it's going to be very difficult for them to exclude Spain and Italy...and that will be keeping the mark on the defensive," Bank of America's Hayward said.
"That will remain the case as long as there isn't another shock, like a breakdown in talks," he said.

Meanwhile, some said the markets were no longer disturbed about the French demands on the stability pact because although it was seen as a stumbling block, it was not as big a problem as some other issues hanging over EMU.
"It shows people don't rate the French problem as gravely as they do Germany's difficulties (such as its budget deficit) and the splits in Germany's ruling coalition," Chase's Marshall said.
